content: Individuals with minimal liver fibrosis and a low risk of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) progression do not require antiviral therapy. Prospective studies have identified several predictors of progression in HBV-related liver disease, including the risk of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and CHB exacerbations. These predictors include age, gender, serum ALT levels, ongoing HBV replication (measured by serum HBV DNA levels), HBV genotype, HBV pre-core and core promoter variants, family history of HCC, and cofactors such as alcohol use, HIV infection, and diabetes. The purpose of the evidence review was twofold: first, to determine which factors or tests among HBsAg-positive individuals best identify those at the highest and lowest risk of disease progression; and second, to identify individuals who would derive the greatest or least benefit from treatment, particularly in settings with or without access to HBV DNA testing. Baseline prognostic factors included age (e.g., >40 or >30 years vs. <40 or <30 years), cirrhosis or fibrosis stage (e.g., METAVIR stages 1–3 vs. no cirrhosis or fibrosis), ALT levels (e.g., >2x or >5x the upper limit of normal [ULN] vs. normal), and HBV DNA levels (e.g., >2000 IU/mL or >20,000 IU/mL vs. undetectable). Key outcomes included liver-related mortality and morbidity (e.g., fibrosis, cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, HCC) and progression of liver disease. A systematic review of 22 observational studies, including large population-based prospective cohort studies, provided evidence on predictors of disease progression. Most studies were conducted in Asia, with some in Europe, North America, and the Middle/Near East. The populations analyzed included HBeAg-positive, HBeAg-negative, and HIV-coinfected individuals. The REVEAL-HBV cohort, a large population-based study in Taiwan, provided high-quality evidence on patient-important outcomes such as HCC, liver cirrhosis, and liver-related deaths. It demonstrated a consistent and linear increase in HCC incidence with baseline HBV DNA levels >10,000 copies/mL (>2000 IU/mL), even in HBeAg-negative individuals, regardless of cirrhosis or ALT levels. Additional studies showed that male gender, increasing age, and elevated HBV DNA and ALT levels were associated with an increased risk of liver-related outcomes. Persistently normal ALT levels were associated with a low probability of advanced fibrosis, while abnormal ALT levels (e.g., >2x ULN) were linked to an increased risk of cirrhosis. Evidence from systematic reviews highlighted that age >40 years and ALT levels >5x ULN were significant predictors of hepatitis reactivation in HBeAg-positive individuals. Among HBeAg-negative individuals, HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/mL were predictive of current fibrosis and future active hepatitis. The quality of evidence from population-based studies was rated as moderate to high for mortality and HCC outcomes but low for liver cirrhosis or fibrosis due to imprecision and reliance on clinical criteria or ultrasound without liver biopsy. There were no data from sub-Saharan Africa or Latin America, and the REVEAL study findings may not apply to individuals with adult-acquired HBV infection, those aged <30 or >65 years, or those infected with non-B or C HBV genotypes. There were also no studies in pregnant women, children, or adolescents with CHB. Limited data exist on HBV/HIV-coinfected individuals, with one retrospective cohort study showing that baseline CD4+ cell count <200 cells/mm³, ALT elevation, and detectable HIV RNA were associated with an increased risk of advanced liver disease. Evidence for treatment benefit in individuals with advanced liver disease showed that continuous lamivudine therapy reduced the incidence of hepatic decompensation and HCC by 55%. Entecavir-treated patients had a 50–70% reduced risk of clinical outcomes, including HCC and liver-related mortality, compared to untreated individuals with cirrhosis. Tenofovir therapy demonstrated improvements in necroinflammation and fibrosis over five years. The Guidelines Development Group recommended prioritizing antiviral therapy for individuals with life-threatening liver disease (e.g., decompensated cirrhosis) and compensated cirrhosis, regardless of ALT or HBV DNA levels. Antiviral therapy can halve disease progression and may lead to regression of fibrosis and cirrhosis over the long term. Treatment decisions in non-cirrhotic individuals should target those at the highest risk of disease progression, particularly those with persistently abnormal ALT levels and HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, especially in individuals aged >30 years. In settings without access to HBV DNA testing, treatment decisions rely on clinical features, non-invasive tests (NITs), and serum ALT levels. However, NITs like APRI and transient elastography have low positive predictive value for identifying cirrhosis. The group recommended initiating treatment in individuals with persistently abnormal ALT levels after excluding other causes, while treatment was not recommended for HBeAg-negative individuals aged <30 years with persistently normal ALT levels. Continued monitoring is required for individuals who do not meet treatment criteria.
